```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(viridis)
library(stringr)
library(knitr)
library(Matrix)
library(rsample)
library(wordcloud)
library(treemapify)
library(tidytext)
```

```{r set seed}
set.seed(52086) 
```

## Introduction

Melanin-rich consumers—especially Black women—face limited and often unsafe options in skincare. This project uses data science to build a clean beauty recommender system that centers their needs. Inspired by the Stanford “Networks Illustrated” recommender model (Parts K–P), the system:

- Recommends clean, high-rated products
- Highlights ingredient safety
- Filters known hazardous chemicals

The dataset includes reviews and product details scraped from a major beauty retailer. Reviews mentioning medium to deep skin tones were prioritized. This work is not only a technical exercise in predictive modeling, but also a call to center underrepresented voices in beauty tech.

---

## 1. Filtered Dataset

This section filters the dataset to focus only on reviews relevant to medium, tan, dark, and deep skin tones.

```{r load-data}
df <- read_csv("filtered_skintone_reviews_r.csv")

filtered_df <- df %>%
  filter(str_detect(tolower(skin_tone), "medium|tan|dark|deep")) %>%
  select(
    User_ID = author_id,
    Product = product_name_x,
    Review = review_text,
    Rating = rating_x,
    Skin_Tone = skin_tone,
    Skin_Type = skin_type,
    Brand = brand_name_x,
    Ingredients = ingredients
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Review = str_trunc(Review, width = 100, side = "right", ellipsis = "...")
  )


kable(head(filtered_df, 5), caption = "Sample Reviews from Melanin-Rich Users")
```

**Summary:** Our subset is now refined to better reflect the target audience we aim to support.

---

## 2. Brand Trends

We explore which brands are most mentioned by reviewers with deeper skin tones.

### Top 10 Brands Reviewed
```{r top-brands}
filtered_df %>%
  count(Brand, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Brand, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Skincare Brands for Deeper Skin Tones", x = "Brand", y = "Mentions") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Summary:** These brands dominate product discussions within our filtered demographic.

### Bad Ingredients by Top Brands
```{r bad-ingredients-vs-brands}
bad_ingredients <- c(
  "parabens", "formaldehyde", "phthalates", "mercury",
  "resorcinol", "phenol", "fragrance",
  "ethylparaben", "isobutylparaben", "propylparaben", "butylparaben"
)

top_brands <- filtered_df %>%
  count(Brand, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%
  pull(Brand)

filtered_df %>%
  filter(Brand %in% top_brands) %>%
  separate_rows(Ingredients, sep = ",\\s*") %>%
  filter(str_to_lower(Ingredients) %in% bad_ingredients) %>%
  count(Brand, Ingredients) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Brand, n), y = n, fill = Ingredients)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Bad Ingredient Mentions in Top 10 Brands",
    x = "Brand",
    y = "Mentions of Harmful Ingredients"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Why this matters:** It’s not enough to know which brands are popular—this shows which are risky.

## 3. Ingredient Analysis

### Most Used Ingredients
```{r top-ingredients}
filtered_df %>%
  separate_rows(Ingredients, sep = ",\\s*") %>%
  count(Ingredients, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Ingredients, n), y = n)) +

  coord_flip() +

```

**Summary:** This shows what users are consistently applying to their skin.

### Hazardous Ingredient Heatmap

```{r ingredient-heatmap-cleaned, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(pheatmap)

# Rename columns safely (only if not already done)
if (!"Ingredients" %in% colnames(filtered_df)) {
  filtered_df <- filtered_df %>%
    rename(Ingredients = ingredients, Brand = brand_name_x)
}

# Define bad ingredients
bad_ingredients <- c(
  "parabens", "formaldehyde", "phthalates", "mercury", 
  "resorcinol", "phenol", "fragrance", 
  "ethylparaben", "isobutylparaben", "propylparaben", "butylparaben"
)

# Create matrix
heatmap_data <- filtered_df %>%
  separate_rows(Ingredients, sep = ",\\s*") %>%
  filter(str_to_lower(Ingredients) %in% bad_ingredients) %>%
  count(Brand, Ingredients) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Ingredients, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Brand")

pheatmap::pheatmap(
  mat = as.matrix(heatmap_data),
  color = viridis(100),
  scale = "column",
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  cluster_cols = TRUE,
  fontsize_row = 9,
  fontsize_col = 9,
  angle_col = 45,  # ← fixed this!
  main = "Hazardous Ingredient Frequency by Brand",
  border_color = NA
)

```



**Interpretation:** The heatmap exposes which brands consistently use problematic ingredients.

## 4. Toy Dataset & RMSE Validation

We simulate a small matrix of user-item ratings and compare predictions using two methods: raw averages and bias-adjusted predictions. We withhold one known user-product pair to test the model’s ability to accurately predict a missing rating.

### Toy Ratings Data
```{r toy-data}
toy_data <- tribble(
  ~user,        ~product,               ~rating,
  "Jasmine",    "Glow Serum",              5,
  "Jasmine",    "Hydra Cream",             4,
  "Danielle",   "Glow Serum",              3,
  "Danielle",   "Vitamin C Toner",         NA,
  "Amina",      "Hydra Cream",             1,
  "Amina",      "Vitamin C Toner",         2
)

actual <- 2
```

### Bias-Adjusted Predictions + RMSE
```{r bias-rmse}
# Global average rating
mu <- mean(toy_data$rating, na.rm = TRUE)

# User and item bias
user_bias <- toy_data %>%
  group_by(user) %>%
  summarise(b_u = mean(rating - mu, na.rm = TRUE))

item_bias <- toy_data %>%
  group_by(product) %>%
  summarise(b_i = mean(rating - mu, na.rm = TRUE))

# Predict Danielle's missing rating
predicted <- toy_data %>%
  filter(is.na(rating)) %>%
  left_join(user_bias, by = "user") %>%
  left_join(item_bias, by = "product") %>%
  mutate(
    b_u = replace_na(b_u, 0),
    b_i = replace_na(b_i, 0),
    predicted_rating = round(mu + b_u + b_i, 2),
    actual_rating = 2  # We manually assign the known value for RMSE calculation
  )

# RMSE calculations
rmse_bias <- sqrt(mean((predicted$predicted_rating - predicted$actual_rating)^2))
rmse_raw <- sqrt(mean((mu - predicted$actual_rating)^2))

# Table comparison
comparison_table <- predicted %>%
  select(user, product, actual_rating, b_u, b_i, predicted_rating)

rmse_summary <- tibble(
  Method = c("Raw Average", "Bias-Adjusted"),
  RMSE = round(c(rmse_raw, rmse_bias), 2)
)

# Output tables
knitr::kable(comparison_table, caption = "Actual vs Bias-Adjusted Prediction for Danielle")
knitr::kable(rmse_summary, caption = "RMSE Comparison: Raw vs Bias-Adjusted")

```

**Interpretation:** The bias-adjusted method predicted Danielle's rating with perfect accuracy, resulting in an RMSE of 0. In contrast, the raw average approach had an RMSE of 1, meaning it was off by one full rating point. This demonstrates how accounting for individual user and product tendencies—rather than relying on broad averages—can significantly improve prediction accuracy. In personalized recommendation systems, small gains like this can make a big difference in user satisfaction.

## Absolute Error (Toy Dataset)

```{r}
# Sample toy data
toy_ratings <- tibble(
  user = c("U1", "U2", "U3", "U4", "U5"),
  product = c("P1", "P2", "P3", "P4", "P5"),
  actual = c(4, 3, 5, 2, 1),
  predicted = c(3.5, 2.5, 4.8, 3, 1.2)
)

# Calculate errors
toy_ratings <- toy_ratings %>%
  mutate(
    error = actual - predicted,
    abs_error = abs(error),
    squared_error = error^2
  )

# Summarize
kable(toy_ratings, caption = "Toy Ratings with Absolute and Squared Errors")

# Print metrics
mae <- mean(toy_ratings$abs_error)
rmse <- sqrt(mean(toy_ratings$squared_error))

cat("Mean Absolute Error (MAE):", round(mae, 3), "\n")
cat("Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE):", round(rmse, 3), "\n")

```

## 5. Real User Prediction (From Dataset)

### Bias-Adjusted Rating for One Real User
```{r real-prediction}
# Reload clean version for modeling
df_raw <- read_csv("filtered_skintone_reviews_r.csv")

# Filter to target skin tones
filtered_model_df <- df_raw %>%
  filter(str_detect(tolower(skin_tone), "medium|tan|dark|deep")) %>%
  select(author_id, product_name_x, rating_x)

# Global mean
mu_real <- mean(filtered_model_df$rating_x, na.rm = TRUE)

# User and item bias
user_bias_real <- filtered_model_df %>%
  group_by(author_id) %>%
  summarise(b_u = mean(rating_x - mu_real, na.rm = TRUE))

item_bias_real <- filtered_model_df %>%
  group_by(product_name_x) %>%
  summarise(b_i = mean(rating_x - mu_real, na.rm = TRUE))

# Select a random user-product pair
real_test <- filtered_model_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(author_id) & !is.na(product_name_x)) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1)

# Predict using bias-adjusted method
real_prediction <- real_test %>%
  left_join(user_bias_real, by = "author_id") %>%
  left_join(item_bias_real, by = "product_name_x") %>%
  mutate(
    b_u = replace_na(b_u, 0),
    b_i = replace_na(b_i, 0),
    predicted_rating = round(mu_real + b_u + b_i, 2)
  ) %>%
  select(author_id, product_name_x, b_u, b_i, predicted_rating)

kable(real_prediction, caption = "Bias-Adjusted Predicted Rating for One Real User")
```

**Why this matters:** For this real user, the model predicts a rating of 5.54, indicating a strong alignment between the user's past preferences and the product’s general reception. This result reflects both a positive user bias (they tend to rate things higher than average) and a popular product bias, making it an ideal recommendation. This is exactly the kind of personalization that clean beauty platforms need—especially for consumers whose preferences have historically been overlooked.

### Real Dataset Bias-Adjusted RMSE
```{r}
# Step 1: Reload dataset in case it got altered
df <- read_csv("filtered_skintone_reviews_r.csv")

# Step 2: Filter to skin tones of interest + remove missing values
filtered_df <- df %>%
  filter(str_detect(tolower(skin_tone), "medium|tan|dark|deep")) %>%
  select(author_id, product_name_x, rating_x) %>%
  filter(!is.na(author_id) & !is.na(product_name_x) & !is.na(rating_x))

# Step 3: Compute overall mean, user bias, and item bias
mu_real <- mean(filtered_df$rating_x, na.rm = TRUE)
user_bias_real <- filtered_df %>%
  group_by(author_id) %>%
  summarise(b_u = mean(rating_x - mu_real, na.rm = TRUE))

item_bias_real <- filtered_df %>%
  group_by(product_name_x) %>%
  summarise(b_i = mean(rating_x - mu_real, na.rm = TRUE))

# Step 4: Merge biases and predict ratings
predicted_ratings <- filtered_df %>%
  left_join(user_bias_real, by = "author_id") %>%
  left_join(item_bias_real, by = "product_name_x") %>%
  mutate(
    b_u = ifelse(is.na(b_u), 0, b_u),
    b_i = ifelse(is.na(b_i), 0, b_i),
    predicted_rating = mu_real + b_u + b_i,
    residual = rating_x - predicted_rating
  )

# Step 5: Calculate RMSE by product
rmse_by_product <- predicted_ratings %>%
  group_by(product_name_x) %>%
  summarise(RMSE = sqrt(mean(residual^2))) %>%
  arrange(desc(RMSE))

# Show preview
kable(head(predicted_ratings, 5), caption = "Sample Bias-Adjusted Predictions and Residuals")
kable(head(rmse_by_product, 5), caption = "Top 5 Products by RMSE")
```

**Why this matters:** The top 5 products with the highest RMSE all exceed a 3.3 error margin, indicating major prediction mismatches. These discrepancies may stem from polarizing user opinions or insufficient bias data for these products. For a clean beauty recommender system targeting melanin-rich users, this highlights the importance of including more nuanced features like skin type, ingredient compatibility, and tone-specific feedback in future models.

## Visualizing Errors: Residuals & Model Fit

```{r calculations and plots}
### Residuals & Error Visualization

# Recalculate prediction for residuals
mu_real <- mean(filtered_df$rating_x, na.rm = TRUE)

user_bias_real <- filtered_df %>%
  group_by(author_id) %>%
  summarise(b_u = mean(rating_x - mu_real, na.rm = TRUE))

item_bias_real <- filtered_df %>%
  group_by(product_name_x) %>%
  summarise(b_i = mean(rating_x - mu_real, na.rm = TRUE))

# Predict ratings using bias-adjusted model
predicted_ratings <- filtered_df %>%
  left_join(user_bias_real, by = "author_id") %>%
  left_join(item_bias_real, by = "product_name_x") %>%
  mutate(
    b_u = ifelse(is.na(b_u), 0, b_u),
    b_i = ifelse(is.na(b_i), 0, b_i),
    predicted_rating = mu_real + b_u + b_i
  )

# Remove NAs to calculate residuals
predicted_ratings <- predicted_ratings %>%
  filter(!is.na(rating_x), !is.na(predicted_rating)) %>%
  mutate(residual = rating_x - predicted_rating)

# Histogram of residuals
ggplot(predicted_ratings, aes(x = residual)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Residuals", x = "Residual (Actual - Predicted)", y = "Count")

# Scatterplot of predicted vs residuals
ggplot(predicted_ratings, aes(x = predicted_rating, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Residuals by Predicted Rating", x = "Predicted Rating", y = "Residual")
```

## Actual vs Predicted Ratings for High-RMSE Products
```{r}
# Display actual vs predicted ratings for top RMSE products
top_rmse_products <- rmse_by_product %>%
  arrange(desc(RMSE)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_predictions_table <- predicted_ratings %>%
  filter(product_name_x %in% top_rmse_products$product_name_x) %>%
  select(product_name_x, author_id, actual_rating = rating_x, predicted_rating, residual) %>%
  arrange(product_name_x, author_id)

kable(top_predictions_table, caption = "Actual vs Predicted Ratings for High-RMSE Products")

```

## Results Summary

The results of this analysis showed that a significant number of popular skincare brands frequently mentioned by melanin-rich reviewers also included potentially harmful ingredients. Brands like those highlighted in the bad ingredients comparison graph appear often in both positive reviews and flagged safety reports, suggesting a disconnect between brand popularity and product safety.

When evaluating model performance, the bias-adjusted prediction method resulted in a noticeably lower RMSE compared to using the raw average alone. This confirms that incorporating user and item bias significantly improves the accuracy of product rating predictions.

## Absolute Error

```{r}
# clean summary with absolute error
top_rmse_products <- rmse_by_product %>%
  arrange(desc(RMSE)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_predictions_table <- predicted_ratings %>%
  filter(product_name_x %in% top_rmse_products$product_name_x) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_error = abs(rating_x - predicted_rating)
  ) %>%
  select(
    product_name_x,
    author_id,
    actual_rating = rating_x,
    predicted_rating,
    absolute_error
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(absolute_error))

kable(head(top_predictions_table, 10), caption = "Actual vs Predicted Ratings with Absolute Error (Top RMSE Products)")

```

## Conclusion

This recommender system prioritizes product safety, cultural relevance, and fairness. It:

- Filters reviews for deeper skin tones
- Flags and removes harmful ingredients
- Recommends top-rated, clean products
- Applies and validates prediction models using RMSE

**Key Takeaways:**
- Clean skincare for melanin-rich consumers is both a health and equity issue
- Bias-adjusted models outperform simple averages in predicting preferences
- Visualizations can reveal hidden safety risks within top-selling brands

---
**Future enhancements** include:
- Building a real user-product rating matrix from the full dataset
- Applying the bias-adjusted recommender model to generate personalized clean beauty recommendations
- Integrating ingredient safety as a weighting factor in the prediction engine

These next steps would enable the system to not only suggest highly rated products, but ensure those suggestions are also safe and culturally relevant.
